Every factual claim inside it is carried by a precedent row below, each verified against a fetched or snippet-corroborated source (per-source status recorded). Research trail: data/research/orderbook-mechanisms.json. 2026-09-09: clarified the EFI Foundation FOAK-unit figure as a total capital cost per SMR unit (not per kW or per MWh). 2026-09-26: added the group 'Pooled buying and shared risk in other markets' (24 non-nuclear precedents from data/research/2026-09-26-refresh/pooling.json, integrated by that folder's integrate_pooling.py), a mechanism `type` on every precedent, and the proposal card 'What other markets add to the design'.

intro: The first microreactor orders are the expensive ones, so nobody wants to go first. DOE's liftoff analysis says a factory needs 30 to 50 committed units of a single design (about 500 MW), and no single buyer is anywhere near that on their own. A shared orderbook lets buyers pool their orders so none of them carries first-unit risk alone, and an overrun pool settles in advance who pays if a build goes over budget. The three cards below are our own proposal.

cards.title: The shared orderbook
paras: One book across every buyer of a standardized unit class, priced as a blend: each participant pays the same average cost across the whole book, so unit one and unit forty cost the same for the same delivery year. That single choice, used by the EFI Foundation's cost-stabilization facility and DOE's buyers-consortium model, is what removes the incentive to wait for someone braver to go first.

Orders are binding and carry deposits, the instrument Equinix has already executed for 20 microreactor units, because DOE found that all the MOUs and letters of intent in circulation had produced zero signed reactor construction contracts by late 2024. The vendor spreads first-unit engineering across the whole book the way Boeing sold its launch customer 50 aircraft rather than one plane carrying all the 787's design cost.

cards.title: The overrun pool
paras: A layered waterfall, never one blanket guarantee: the project sponsor pays a bounded first band (a deductible), a mutual pool funded by a premium on every order pays the middle band, and a backstop takes only the tail. Every credible design converges on this shape: NIA's deductible plus copayment, EFI's three tiers ending in an automatic federal loan, Virginia's banded overrun schedule for offshore wind, Price-Anderson's two liability layers.

The infrastructure exists. NEIL, the industry's own mutual, already runs a builders-risk program that reinsured Vogtle's construction; a commercial placement covered TerraPower's Kemmerer build in 2026; and the pending ARC Act would add a federal overrun backstop gated on three or more qualifying projects existing. The pool also needs a separately priced provision for economy-wide inflation, because macro shocks broke both UAMPS and NYSERDA's offshore-wind rounds even where real learning was happening.

cards.title: Early orders vs late
paras: Who gets the better deal depends on who is paying. Inside the buyer pool, nobody: the blended price is deliberately flat, so early buyers can never end up worse off and late buyers gain nothing by waiting. Outside subsidy is a different layer, and there the federal precedent front-loads hard: DOE's $900M SMR program gives its two first-mover teams roughly eight times more per project than its fast followers.

Early buyers also take the non-price benefits: first claim on delivery slots, governance seats in the pool, and whatever launch discount the manufacturer funds from its own margin, the aviation pattern of pricing early units below cost to buy down pioneer risk. UAMPS is the cautionary inverse: a symmetric opt-out with no reward for staying meant that when costs rose 53%, the rational member simply left.

cards.title: What other markets add to the design
paras: Each step below is borrowed from a market that has run it, and each named case is a row in the list further down, with its numbers and sources.
steps: A public threshold: orders bind only if a stated number of units clears by a deadline, and the book is capped at what the factory can build (Kickstarter's rule, and Pebble's lesson).
Growth by rule: each block of newly committed offtake orders the next unit, as NATO's tanker pool orders an aircraft for every 1,100 committed flight-hours.
Shares, not whole reactors: a 2 MW buyer holds a slice of a fleet's output, the way twelve nations share three C-17s and NetJets owners draw guaranteed hours from a pool.
An availability fee where firmness is the product, as the NHS pays a fixed yearly sum per antibiotic regardless of doses used.
Prepayments spread across vendors and sites: Apple's single-supplier sapphire prepayment still had $439 million outstanding when the supplier failed.
A layered overrun pool: each project keeps the first slice, the pool pays a capped middle layer, reinsurance takes the top, and a public backstop sits last (P&I clubs, Pool Re, TRIA).
Early tranches priced below the later market, or the first buyers wait, as they did when Bordeaux 2011 futures cost more than bottled older vintages.

items.name: DOE Pathways to Commercial Liftoff — committed orderbook framework
items.mechanism: DOE's flagship framework (2023, updated Sept 2024) makes a committed orderbook the first phase of commercial liftoff: 5–10 units of one design for SMRs, and 30–50 units specifically for microreactors, whose factories must be justified across far smaller per-unit MW. It distinguishes a buyers' consortium (offtakers pool demand at one average price) from a builders' consortium (asset owners spread early costs), and cites Boeing's 787 launch strategy by name.
items.outcome: As of Sept 2024, zero signed contracts to construct new US reactors existed despite many MOUs. The report quantifies the learning it wants to capture: bulk-ordering 10+ reactors could cut first-unit cost ~15%; Vogtle Unit 4 came in ~30% cheaper than Unit 3 on the same site.
items.early_vs_late: Two answers by layer: the buyer pool itself should charge one blended average price ("customers all be 'one fifth' of the orderbook versus 'waiting to be fifth'"), while government incentives on top should be front-loaded: "Ensuring that first-movers receive the best deal could induce customers to commit earlier."
items.relevance: This tab's design comes mostly from here: a flat average inside the pool, front-loaded subsidy outside it, and a 30–50 unit target that makes multi-buyer aggregation mandatory for microreactors.

sources.quote: Ensuring that first-movers receive the best deal could induce customers to commit earlier

items.name: EFI Foundation Cost Stabilization Facility
items.mechanism: Working paper (Oct 2023; model term sheet Jan 2025) for an SMR orderbook of at least 3 projects (illustrated at 10 units): sponsors hold pro-rata interests in every unit through an SPV; sponsors fund the baseline budget and a pooled contingency in full; only when both are exhausted does a DOE backstop loan trigger automatically, illustrated at an 80% federal / 20% sponsor split of the overrun tail.
items.outcome: Proposal only. Illustrative numbers: a 10-unit, $20B orderbook with a $5B (25%) contingency facility; total capital cost per SMR unit (not per kW or per MWh) declines from $2.45B for the FOAK unit to $1.79B for unit 10.
items.early_vs_late: Deliberately flat: "all the participants experience the same average cost based upon the total cost of all the units in the orderbook". The design goal is erasing the first-mover disadvantage so nobody benefits from delaying.
items.relevance: Closest thing to a working blueprint for a shared microreactor orderbook plus risk pool. It pools through an SPV, tiers the contingency, adds an automatic backstop, and gives a reasoned rejection of price differences by order position.

items.name: Nuclear Innovation Alliance — Catalyzing Commitments (June 2024)
items.mechanism: Recommends serial multi-project development to share FOAK costs; offtakers co-funding development in exchange for later compensation; premium offtake pricing until maturity; and, as "the most impactful private-sector action," offtaker capital commitments as a completion-cost backstop. Proposes a deductible (an initial increment of increased costs) plus a copayment (a share of further increases) retained by the sponsor even after any backstop engages, to preserve cost discipline.
items.outcome: Working paper. Notes Google, Microsoft and Nucor had already issued a joint Advanced Clean Electricity RFI (March 2024) signalling advance-commitment interest.
items.early_vs_late: No price tiering by order position; every sponsor keeps skin in the game through the deductible and copayment regardless of vintage.
items.relevance: Supplies the deductible-plus-copayment vocabulary for the overrun pool's first band.

items.name: UAMPS Carbon Free Power Project (NuScale)
items.mechanism: About 27 municipal utilities subscribed to shares of a 6-module NuScale plant under a Budget and Plan of Finance that let any member withdraw, reimbursed for most costs, if $/MWh crossed an agreed ceiling. Continuation required roughly 80% subscription.
items.outcome: Target price rose from $58/MWh (2021) to $89/MWh (2023), a 53% increase, as estimated construction cost climbed from $5.3B to $9.3B. UAMPS and NuScale terminated the project on 2023-11-08 for insufficient subscription.
items.early_vs_late: Symmetric by design: every member had the same opt-out at the same ceiling whenever they joined, so there was no reward for committing early and no cost to waiting, which was a structural driver of the shortfall.
items.relevance: Shows what goes wrong. An opt-out-only pool with no early-mover benefit and no shared overrun backstop dissolves as soon as costs rise.

items.name: DOE $900M Gen III+ SMR solicitation
items.mechanism: DE-FOA-0003485 splits $900M into Tier 1 First Mover Team Support (up to $800M for at most two utility-led teams) and Tier 2 Fast Follower support (about $100M across additional projects), funded by the IIJA and FY2024 appropriations.
items.outcome: Tier 1 awards of $800M announced Dec 2025 to Tennessee Valley Authority and Holtec Government Services.
items.early_vs_late: Explicitly front-loaded, roughly 8× more per project for the first movers than the fast followers, in exchange for bearing FOAK risk.
items.relevance: A live, funded federal example of the outside-subsidy layer paying first movers most, which is what this tab proposes above the flat-priced pool.

items.name: Google–Kairos Power master agreement
items.mechanism: A Master Plant Development Agreement (Oct 2024) covering a fleet of reactors totalling 500 MW by 2035, first unit by 2030; Kairos builds and operates, selling through PPAs under the master framework with milestone-based accountability.
items.outcome: Signed; described as the first US corporate agreement for multiple deployments of a single advanced reactor design. No public per-unit price schedule.
items.early_vs_late: Undisclosed; Kairos frames the fleet structure as the way to move down the learning curve toward cost and schedule certainty.
items.relevance: A buyers' club of one, where a single hyperscaler aggregates its own multi-unit demand to reach fleet pricing. The shared orderbook generalises this across many smaller buyers.

sources.label: Kairos Power — Google partnership announcement
sources.quote: the first corporate agreement for multiple deployments of a single advanced reactor design in the United States

items.name: Equinix–Radiant 20-unit preorder
items.mechanism: A preorder with paid deposits for 20 Kaleidos microreactors (announced 2025-08-14), ahead of the design's first fuelled test at INL's DOME facility.
items.outcome: Radiant calls it the largest deal to date for any mass-manufactured reactor. No public per-unit price or delivery schedule.
items.early_vs_late: Undisclosed; nothing public says whether Equinix's price falls if later buyers join Radiant's book.
items.relevance: Real deposits on 20 units still fall short of DOE's 30–50 unit factory threshold, which is the concrete case for aggregating several such buyers into one book.

sources.quote: This agreement with Equinix demonstrates the critical need to deliver dependable power anywhere it's needed

items.name: DOE Advanced Reactor Demonstration Program
items.mechanism: 50/50 public-private cost share awarded 2020: about $2B toward TerraPower's Natrium and $1.2B toward X-energy's Xe-100, industry matching dollar-for-dollar, $3.2B DOE total over seven years.
items.outcome: Both demonstrations underway as of 2026; single-project awards, no multi-buyer structure.
items.early_vs_late: One FOAK project per design; the question does not arise.
items.relevance: Both NIA and EFI cite this as necessary and insufficient. It de-risks the first plant but aggregates no demand and pools no overrun risk, which is the gap this tab's mechanism fills.

items.name: GAVI pneumococcal Advance Market Commitment
items.mechanism: Donors pledged $1.5B (2009) to guarantee manufacturers a price: suppliers committed for 10 years to a $3.50/dose tail price and received a $3.50/dose top-up on roughly the first 20% of doses supplied, funded from the shared pool.
items.outcome: 161M doses procured through the AMC in 2019; 1.65B doses contracted through 2027; three vaccines developed and over 150M children immunised.
items.early_vs_late: Uniform: every qualifying dose in the subsidized tranche earned the same top-up regardless of when the supplier joined; the subsidy tracked volume share, never arrival order.
items.relevance: A flat, volume-proportional subsidy, and one of the three distinct answers the precedents give to who should get the better deal.

sources.quote: per dose for approximately 20% of the doses they provide

items.name: Frontier climate advance market commitment
items.mechanism: Launched 2022 by Stripe, Alphabet, Shopify, Meta and McKinsey at $1B+ (later $1.8B): low-volume prepurchases for early-stage suppliers and offtakes for growth-stage ones, with prices deliberately higher for earlier, riskier tons.
items.outcome: $1.8B committed; funded early deals from Charm Industrial onward through 2025.
items.early_vs_late: Inverted on purpose: early suppliers are paid more per ton as a market-making subsidy, pulling the cost curve down for everyone who buys later.
items.relevance: Shows that paying more early can be the rational design when the goal is to create supply that does not exist yet.

sources.label: Frontier — an advance market commitment to accelerate carbon removal
sources.quote: buyers will enter into low-volume prepurchase agreements

items.name: First Movers Coalition
items.mechanism: WEF and the US government coordinate forward purchasing pledges: members commit a percentage of future procurement (green steel, aluminium, cement, shipping, aviation, CDR) by a target year, with no single binding master contract.
items.outcome: 101 companies had pledged $19B in purchasing commitments by 2030, per WEF's 2024 reporting.
items.early_vs_late: No price differentiation; the early-pledger benefit is influence over which suppliers and technologies get validated.
items.relevance: A lightweight on-ramp. A microreactor buyers' club could start as percentage pledges and harden into binding preorders later, as long as it does harden: DOE found that soft pledges alone produced zero signed contracts.

sources.label: WEF — First Movers Coalition 2024 commitments

items.name: Boeing 787 launch-customer economics
items.mechanism: Boeing launched the 787 with All Nippon Airways ordering 50 aircraft (2004, list value ~$6B, heavily discounted). Aircraft makers price early units below production cost and recoup after cumulative volume drives unit cost past break-even; aerospace learning curves run 80–90%.
items.outcome: Program reached full commercial scale; over 1,000 787s delivered since.
items.early_vs_late: The launch customer gets the steepest discount, funded by the manufacturer against future volume, as compensation for bearing pioneer risk on an unproven airframe.
items.relevance: DOE's Liftoff report cites this precedent by name. It is the template for a manufacturer-funded early discount, where the maker pays for it and the later buyers do not.

sources.label: DOE Liftoff report — Boeing 787 analogy
sources.quote: Boeing sold 50 787s to their first customer, spreading early costs over multiple planes in a single order

items.name: Operation Warp Speed advance purchases
items.mechanism: The US government combined R&D funding, manufacturing subsidies and advance purchase agreements so vaccine makers could build capacity before trial results existed; Pfizer took a pure $1.95B APA for 100M doses with no federal R&D money.
items.outcome: Roughly $10–18B deployed; vaccines reached market in under a year against a typical decade.
items.early_vs_late: A single government buyer shifting risk off manufacturers; no multi-buyer price question arises.
items.relevance: How to fund factory tooling ahead of a full book: one deep-pocketed backstop pays for at-risk capacity. That maps to the federal loan layer, never to the buyer pool.

items.name: DOE SunShot Initiative
items.mechanism: A 2011 program targeting a 75% cut in solar costs by 2020, pursued through R&D and soft-cost reduction (permitting, financing, installation), with no demand-aggregation purchase mechanism at all.
items.outcome: The $0.06/kWh utility-scale target was hit in 2017, three years early, from ~$0.28/kWh in 2011.
items.early_vs_late: No buyer pool existed; the question does not arise.
items.relevance: A reminder that an orderbook is only one lever. If manufacturing and soft costs dominate, a cost curve can move without any buyer-side pooling.

sources.label: DOE — SunShot Initiative
sources.quote: achieved SunShot's original 2020 cost target of $0.06 per kilowatt-hour for utility-scale photovoltaic (PV) solar power three years ahead of schedule

items.name: NYSERDA offshore wind solicitations
items.mechanism: New York procures offshore wind in sequential competitive rounds, each locking a 25-year strike price, on the assumption that successive rounds ratchet prices down.
items.outcome: Prices rose instead: the 2023 round averaged $96.72/MWh (2023 real dollars, $145.07 nominal); the 2024 round averaged $150.15/MWh all-in. Developers holding already-awarded 2023 contracts petitioned for 27–66% price relief citing inflation.
items.early_vs_late: Each round priced independently at that round's market level, so later buyers paid more; 2022–24 interest-rate and supply-chain inflation overwhelmed technology learning.
items.relevance: The macro warning. A pool needs an explicit, separately priced provision for economy-wide inflation, or a good design still fails on a bad macro draw. The same shock broke UAMPS.

items.name: Sematech
items.mechanism: 14 US semiconductor makers formed Sematech in 1987 with DARPA providing $100M/year matched by industry, pooling R&D that members had been duplicating; government matching ended after 1996 by board decision.
items.outcome: Analysis found membership cut members' own private R&D by roughly $300M/year, about three times the subsidy, by removing duplication; the consortium outlived its federal funding.
items.early_vs_late: Simultaneous member-competitors, no order positions.
items.relevance: Answers how long a public backstop should last: government capital can be transitional, sunsetting once the standardized fleet has de-risked itself.

items.name: Kickstarter all-or-nothing crowdfunding (Pebble smartwatch)
items.mechanism: Backers pledge a card-on-file amount against a fixed dollar goal and a fixed deadline; if the goal isn't reached, no backer is charged and the project gets nothing, which is the textbook 'assurance contract' solution to a threshold public-goods problem. Pebble cleared its $100,000 threshold within about two hours and kept collecting pledges for the rest of the campaign window, so Kickstarter released the full amount to Pebble as one lump sum rather than per-unit escrow. Backers got a unit once production shipped instead of cash back, so the guarantee each backer bought was that their money would never be spent unless enough other buyers joined.
items.outcome: Pebble asked for $100,000, raised $1 million in the first 28 hours, passed $3 million within a month, and closed having raised over $10 million, proof that the threshold mechanism can recruit far more buyers than the seller expected. Where it broke: The volume the assurance contract attracted outstripped Pebble's ability to execute: the company folded within about four years, and when Fitbit acquired its software/IP in December 2016, unfulfilled orders for the Pebble 2 and Pebble Core were cancelled outright and refunded rather than shipped.
items.relevance: Make every order void unless a stated number of units clears a public bar by a deadline, and cap the book at what the factory can deliver, since Pebble's orders outran its supply chain.

items.name: Tesla Model 3 refundable $1,000 reservations
items.mechanism: Buyers pay a small, fully refundable deposit to reserve a production slot rather than the car itself; the deposit buys queue position, not a locked price or delivery date, and can be pulled back in full at any time before the car is built. Tesla used the running reservation count as a live, public demand signal to justify production investment before a single Model 3 existed. Because deposits were refundable, Tesla carried the volume risk (whether reservation-holders would actually convert to buyers at delivery) while depositors carried none of the price or delivery-date risk.
items.outcome: Tesla said it had over 115,000 reservations in the first 24 hours, 232,000 within two days, and over 325,000 within one week of the March 31, 2016 unveiling, worth over $14 billion in potential sales; Tesla kept the refundable structure for about two years before shifting new US/Canada reservations to a non-refundable $2,500 deposit.
items.relevance: A refundable deposit turns interest into a public, dollar-denominated count a vendor can show its lenders before it builds capacity.

items.name: Bordeaux en primeur wine futures
items.mechanism: Chateaux sell each vintage as a 'future' about 18-24 months before the wine is bottled and delivered, at an opening price the chateau itself sets; buyers prepay in full for an allocation on the bet that the eventual retail price will be higher than the futures price. The chateau captures early cash flow and shifts price risk for an unfinished, unbottled product onto the buyer; there is no collective threshold, no pooled refund fund, and no protection if the retail price two years later turns out lower than what was prepaid.
items.outcome: For the widely panned 2011 vintage, several chateaux still priced their futures 8-15% above the same chateau's already-bottled 2008 vintage sitting on retail shelves, so buyers who prepaid gained nothing versus simply waiting; Chateau Latour announced the 2011 vintage would be its last en primeur offering and left the futures system entirely afterward. Where it broke: The prepayment carried full price risk with no refund path: buyers who locked in 2011 futures priced above prevailing retail levels for older vintages had no recourse, and the mismatch was severe enough that one of Bordeaux's five first growths quit the futures system rather than keep selling into it.
items.relevance: Early tranches have to be priced below what a buyer could get by waiting, or the buyers who prepay first simply stop coming back.

items.name: Apple's $578 million prepayment to GT Advanced Technologies for sapphire
items.mechanism: Apple prepaid GTAT in four installments to fund the capital cost of a dedicated sapphire-furnace factory before a single usable panel had shipped, in exchange for exclusivity and a multi-year supply commitment, with the final $139 million installment released only if GTAT hit unspecified 'operational targets.' GTAT was contracted to repay the prepayment over five years starting in 2015 out of production proceeds, making Apple the plant's financier as well as its customer. Because the money was a repayable prepayment rather than equity or a grant, GTAT alone carried the production-yield risk; Apple's exposure was to GTAT's solvency, not to sapphire prices.
items.outcome: GTAT filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy on October 6, 2014, after it missed the operational targets tied to Apple's final installment and sapphire was left out of the iPhone 6 line entirely; the settlement freed GTAT from its Apple exclusivity and repaid Apple the $439 million outstanding balance, interest-free, from the proceeds of selling off the furnaces. Apple recovered its cash, but the sapphire-manufacturing venture the prepayment funded was liquidated. Where it broke: The prepayment concentrated volume and technology risk in one undiversified supplier: when GTAT couldn't hit the yield and cost targets implied by the contract, the whole facility failed at once, taking the prepayment's intended purpose down with it; a single-supplier prepayment has no diversification against exactly the execution risk it was meant to buy down.
items.relevance: Spread prepayments across more than one vendor or site: a single first-of-a-kind supplier that misses its yield takes the whole prepayment down with it.

items.name: NetJets fractional business-jet ownership
items.mechanism: A buyer purchases a fractional share of a specific aircraft rather than a whole plane, paying an upfront capital cost for the share plus a monthly management fee and hourly flight cost. NetJets pools every owner's aircraft into one operating fleet and guarantees each owner a set number of hours per year on demand, dispatching whichever tail is available rather than 'the' aircraft the owner nominally holds a share of. NetJets, not the individual owner, therefore carries the fleet-utilization and scheduling risk across the whole pool.
items.outcome: The category NetJets pioneered in 1987 has grown into a combined fleet of 792 aircraft (April 2025) guaranteeing owners 50-400 flight hours a year depending on share size, on as little as four hours' notice, letting thousands of buyers who could not justify a whole aircraft's utilization still get one on short notice.
items.relevance: Sell guaranteed output from a pooled fleet rather than a named unit, so a fractional owner draws on whichever reactor is running.

items.name: Strategic Airlift Capability C-17 pool
items.mechanism: Each nation buys into the pool rather than a specific tail number and draws flight hours according to its pre-agreed share; the aircraft are based at Papa Air Base, Hungary and flown under Hungarian military registration no matter which member is using them that day. A single multinational unit schedules, crews and maintains all 3 aircraft for all 12 owners, so no member nation needs its own maintenance and training pipeline to access strategic airlift.
items.outcome: 12 nations that individually could not justify buying or maintaining even one C-17 have had guaranteed, proportional access to a shared 3-aircraft strategic airlift fleet since 2008, with costs and flight hours allocated according to each nation's pre-agreed commitment rather than equal split.
items.relevance: Twelve nations share three aircraft by pre-agreed hours: small buyers can hold a percentage of a fleet they could never own a whole unit of.

items.name: NATO Multinational MRTT Fleet (MMF)
items.category: aviation (aerial refueling fleet, asset-sharing mechanics only)
items.mechanism: Member nations sign a single memorandum of understanding and NATO itself takes title to the aircraft, rather than any one nation owning a tail and leasing it to the others; NSPA runs one multinational squadron that schedules, crews and maintains the whole fleet for every member. Instead of buying aircraft in fixed lot sizes, the programme scales by a hard, pre-published rule: it orders another A330 MRTT only once members' collective flight-hour commitments cross a 1,100-hour increment, so fleet growth tracks demonstrated demand rather than a single member's guess.
items.outcome: From a two-nation MoU in 2012, the pooled fleet had grown to 12 aircraft by 2025 as more nations joined and flight-hour commitments accumulated past the 1,100-hour ordering thresholds, giving members air-refueling and transport capacity none of them could have funded and staffed alone.
items.relevance: Grow the fleet by rule: each block of newly committed offtake triggers the next unit order, the way every 1,100 committed flight-hours orders another tanker.

items.name: Civica Rx hospital-owned generic drug manufacturer
items.mechanism: Member hospitals do not just buy from Civica, they co-own it, and each signs a long-term purchase and supply contract with the company that commits to buying an agreed volume over years rather than shopping the spot generics market. Those long-term commitments are what let Civica plan and finance its own manufacturing capacity (it targets six months of extra inventory as a shortage buffer) instead of relying on the boom-bust order patterns that push ordinary generic makers out of low-margin drugs.
items.outcome: From seven founding health systems in 2018, Civica now supplies more than 80 generic drugs to 55 health systems and 1,500 hospitals (about a third of all U.S. hospital beds) and has distributed over 210 million vials or syringes, addressing the chronic generic-drug shortages the members previously experienced separately.
items.relevance: Tie each member's ownership stake to a multi-year purchase commitment sized to its own demand; that pairing is what finances the shared supplier.

items.name: New York Proton Center hospital consortium
items.mechanism: Three New York hospital systems that otherwise compete for cancer patients co-invested in a single $300 million proton-therapy facility because none of them could individually justify the capital cost and patient volume needed to run it alone. Each partner refers its own patients to the shared machine and shares in its capital and operating costs, rather than each system trying to build a smaller, separately underutilized proton unit.
items.outcome: The consortium delivered New York State's first proton therapy center, a $300 million facility that opened in East Harlem on June 7, 2019, giving all three systems' patients access to equipment none of the three systems had been able to justify building alone.
items.relevance: Competitors can co-own one expensive machine when each would otherwise buy an underused one of its own.

items.name: Pacaso luxury home co-ownership
items.mechanism: Pacaso buys a single-family vacation home, places it in an LLC, and sells shares of that LLC (up to eight per home) to buyers who each get a proportional number of weeks of use per year; Pacaso itself handles furnishing, scheduling and property management across all owners, functioning like NetJets for houses instead of jets. Because each home is capped at eight owners rather than sold as a single-owner property, many local zoning codes written around single-family or timeshare definitions do not clearly cover it.
items.outcome: Multiple California and other resort towns (including Carmel, Palm Springs and St. Helena) issued cease-and-desist orders or sued Pacaso over whether its model is an illegal timeshare under single-family zoning; the St. Helena suit, filed in 2021, settled in February 2024 with Pacaso capped at the four homes it already managed there and barred from adding more without further city approval. Where it broke: Fractionalizing ownership into 8 shares was enough to trigger the exact regulatory classification (timeshare) the structure was designed to avoid in multiple cities, and the resulting litigation capped Pacaso's local growth by negotiated settlement rather than by market demand.
items.relevance: Settle the legal form of fractional ownership with the regulator first; counting co-owners was enough for towns to reclassify Pacaso homes and cap its growth.

items.name: 2Africa submarine cable consortium
items.mechanism: Eight competing telecom operators co-invest directly in one shared cable system instead of each building or leasing separate capacity, splitting the fixed cost of laying 45,000 km of cable across all eight balance sheets. Each member's ownership stake converts into a claim on a share of total system capacity, which it can carry on its own network or resell wholesale, including to non-owners, via an indefeasible right of use (IRU), a long-term prepaid lease on specific fiber capacity. Because the same operators repeat this structure across many cable systems, no single company carries any one cable's full construction and stranding risk alone.
items.outcome: The consortium built the longest subsea cable system in the world: 45,000 km linking 46 landing stations in 33 countries with 180 Tbps of design capacity, with stakes large enough that stc alone disclosed a $205 million investment in just one branch of the system.
items.relevance: Turn an ownership share into a resellable capacity right, so a member with more contracted MW than it needs can sell the surplus.

items.name: NHS England antimicrobial products subscription ('Netflix model')
items.mechanism: NHS England pays each company a fixed annual fee, set in advance from the drug's estimated value to the health service, for unlimited access to the drug, decoupling the company's revenue from how many packs are actually prescribed. This delinks the incentive to sell more antibiotics (which drives resistance) from the incentive to keep developing new ones, since the manufacturer is paid the same fee however many patients the drug treats that year (NHS England estimated about 1,700 a year would be eligible for the first two drugs). NHS bears no volume risk and the manufacturer bears no revenue risk from low prescribing.
items.outcome: The 2022 pilot committed up to £10 million a year to each of two antimicrobials; NHS England judged it enough of a success to tender an expanded program on 12 August 2024 worth up to £1.9 billion over 16 years, capped at £20 million per drug per year, for contracts beginning April 2026.
items.relevance: Pay a fixed annual availability fee instead of a per-MWh price where the buyer is paying for firmness it hopes never to use.

items.name: PAHO Revolving Fund for Access to Vaccines
items.mechanism: Member countries commit their national vaccine and health-supply demand to PAHO instead of procuring individually; PAHO aggregates it into single tenders, letting even small Caribbean states buy at close to the unit price a much larger single buyer would get. A rotating capital fund (the 'revolving' part) lets PAHO pay manufacturers promptly while member countries reimburse the fund on their own budget cycles, decoupling the manufacturer's payment timing from any one country's payment delays.
items.outcome: PAHO's Regional Revolving Funds procured over $800 million in vaccines, medicines and health technology in 2024, with 32 countries and territories now sourcing at least 80% of their total vaccine and supply need through the mechanism rather than buying alone.
items.relevance: A revolving fund pays the vendor on schedule while members repay on their own budget cycles, so no single small buyer carries the timing.

items.name: Global Fund Pooled Procurement Mechanism (PPM)
items.mechanism: Grant implementers in dozens of countries submit their HIV, TB and malaria commodity needs to the Global Fund instead of each negotiating separately with manufacturers; the Fund aggregates the volumes into single negotiations for price and delivery terms, so small countries' orders ride on the purchasing power of the combined total. The mechanism also lets non-Global-Fund money buy through the same negotiated terms, so a country's own domestic budget can extend the pool's pricing beyond Global-Fund-financed purchases.
items.outcome: In 2025 the mechanism managed about $1.02 billion in orders on behalf of grant implementers in 81 countries.

items.name: Louisiana hepatitis C 'Netflix model' subscription
items.mechanism: Instead of paying a per-prescription price for a drug that can cost tens of thousands of dollars per patient, Louisiana pays Asegua one fixed amount for 5 years in exchange for unlimited access to a generic antiviral, so the state's total drug bill no longer scales with how many patients it treats. That flips the incentive from rationing treatment to conserve budget toward treating as many patients as clinical capacity allows, since one more patient treated adds nothing to the bill. Asegua in turn gets a guaranteed multi-year revenue stream instead of per-unit sales that would shrink as the treatable population is cured down over time.
items.outcome: Louisiana's Department of Health finalized the 5-year subscription agreement with Asegua in 2019 for unlimited generic Epclusa access across Medicaid and its prison population, converting an open-ended per-patient drug budget into one fixed, budgetable line item regardless of how many people the state's clinics actually treat.
items.relevance: A fixed multi-year payment for unlimited access suits a buyer whose goal is maximum deployment rather than rationing.

items.name: Rolls-Royce TotalCare power-by-the-hour engine coverage
items.mechanism: Under TotalCare, an airline pays Rolls-Royce a fixed amount per engine flying hour instead of paying for maintenance events as they occur; that per-hour rate is meant to already price in Rolls-Royce's expected shop-visit and unscheduled-removal costs across its whole fleet of that engine type, transferring both time-on-wing and shop-visit cost risk from every individual airline onto Rolls-Royce. Rolls-Royce, not any one airline, therefore carries the tail risk if the engine type needs far more maintenance than priced in; there is no separate reinsurance layer or reserve fund behind the manufacturer's own balance sheet.
items.outcome: When corrosion-related cracking emerged in the Trent 1000's turbine blades fleet-wide, Rolls-Royce, not its airline customers, absorbed the cost under TotalCare: a £554 million exceptional charge, a £1.26 billion first-half pre-tax loss, and total in-service costs that eventually ran past £2 billion ($2.704 billion), while Dreamliner groundings peaked at close to 50 aircraft in 2018. Where it broke: A performance-cover mechanism priced for normal wear transferred a systemic design-and-manufacturing failure onto the single manufacturer's balance sheet with no reinsurance layer behind it. When the fault turned out to be fleet-wide rather than isolated, the manufacturer had underpriced the very risk the contract was built to cover.
items.relevance: A vendor-backed performance guarantee needs reinsurance or a reserve behind it; a fleet-wide defect put more than £2 billion on one balance sheet.

items.name: H2Global / Hintco double-auction mechanism
items.mechanism: Hintco runs a double auction: on the supply side it signs long-term, roughly 10-year fixed-price purchase agreements with the most competitive renewable-hydrogen-derivative producers, giving them bankable revenue certainty; on the demand side it resells the same volumes through short-term sales agreements to whichever industrial buyers bid the highest price. Because early-market production costs exceed what industrial buyers will currently pay, a gap between the purchase and sale price is expected by design, and that 'cost of difference' is covered by a public subsidy pool rather than by the producer or the buyer, so neither counterparty carries the price-gap risk, only the funder does.
items.outcome: Hintco's first pilot auction concluded in 2024 with a maximum contract value of €397 million awarded to Fertiglobe for renewable ammonia deliveries; a second, larger auction round with a budget of up to €3 billion followed, with Germany and the Netherlands jointly committing up to €2.5 billion toward it.
items.relevance: Split the intermediary into a long-term fixed-price buy side and a short-term market sell side, with a public fund paying only the gap.

items.name: Sustainable Aviation Buyers Alliance (SABA) collective SAF certificate purchases
items.mechanism: No individual corporate buyer uses enough jet fuel to negotiate directly with a SAF producer or airline, so SABA pools many buyers' purchase intent into one collective RFP; members then jointly buy 'book-and-claim' certificates representing real SAF supplied into the fuel system elsewhere, decoupling the environmental-attribute purchase from having to physically fuel at a SAF-producing airport. Members don't split a single tank of fuel; each buyer's share of the certificates is sized to, and paid for according to, its own stated volume commitment in the RFP.
items.outcome: SABA's first collective purchase in 2023 covered certificates for 850,000 gallons of SAF; a follow-on multi-year procurement scaled that to close to 20 corporate buyers channeling close to $200 million into roughly 50 million gallons of SAF certificates, about 500,000 tons of abated CO2e.

items.name: Zero Emission Maritime Buyers Alliance (ZEMBA) collective tender
items.mechanism: No single cargo owner ships enough containers on one route to induce a carrier to run a dedicated low-emission service, so ZEMBA aggregates many shippers' forecast container volumes into a single RFP a carrier can answer with one committed service. Hapag-Lloyd won by committing a waste-based biomethane service cutting emissions over 90% versus fossil fuel on the Singapore-Rotterdam lane; each member's share of the committed volume is sized to, and paid for according to, the container-miles it pledged into the tender, not split evenly.
items.outcome: ZEMBA's inaugural tender, launched September 2023 and completed April 2024, locked in Hapag-Lloyd for over 1 billion twenty-foot container-miles of greater-than-90%-lower-emission shipping across 2025-2026, expected to avoid at least 82,000 metric tons of CO2e over the two years.
items.relevance: A collective tender commits a volume before any member's own order exists, giving the vendor one bankable multi-year contract.

items.name: Maschinenring (machinery ring) farm equipment and labor sharing
items.mechanism: A farmer who owns a piece of expensive equipment (a combine, a specialized sprayer) lists it as available through the local ring; a farmer who needs that equipment for a few days but can't justify owning one himself books it and pays the ring, which pays the owning farmer and keeps a coordination fee. The same farmer is typically both a provider (renting out equipment or labor he owns) and a customer (renting what he doesn't) across a season, so the ring nets out each member's use against their supply rather than requiring every member to buy every machine. No central entity owns the equipment; the ring only owns the matching, scheduling and billing layer.
items.outcome: What began as 1960s farmer self-help has scaled to about 240 local rings representing roughly 192,000 farms in Germany alone plus more than 80 rings in Austria, with the coordinating organization now employing 2,500 people just to run the booking and billing layer that connects them.
items.relevance: A broker layer that matches idle capacity to occasional users can run without owning any machines; a host network could do the same with spare heat or power.

items.name: Pool Re UK terrorism reinsurance mutual
items.mechanism: Pool Re reinsures its member insurers' entire book of UK commercial terrorism risk, not policy by policy: each member pays one annual premium and picks a retention level, and Pool Re pays whatever exceeds that retention, with terrorism losses that fall within scheme rules automatically covered without individual declaration. Pool Re itself then buys retrocession cover in the private reinsurance market (£2.3 billion placed with 50-plus reinsurers) before the uncapped HM Treasury guarantee behind it is ever touched, so the sequence is member retention, then Pool Re's own retrocession, then the state, strictly in that order.
items.outcome: Founded in 1993 after the Baltic Exchange and Bishopsgate bombings made commercial terrorism cover commercially unavailable, Pool Re has grown to place a £2.3 billion retrocession programme with more than 50 international reinsurers, with the government's uncapped guarantee behind it never yet called upon since the scheme's launch.
items.relevance: Put the public guarantee last: member retention, then the pool's own reinsurance, then the state, and only for losses the first two cannot cover.

items.name: Terrorism Risk Insurance Act (TRIA) federal backstop
items.mechanism: TRIA requires two separate thresholds before any government money moves: a single act must be certified as terrorism (over $5 million in insured losses), and the whole industry's aggregate certified losses for the year must separately exceed $200 million. Only above both thresholds does the federal government start reimbursing 80% of each individual insurer's losses above its own deductible, and only up to a hard $100 billion cap on total federal exposure, beyond which insurers and policyholders are on their own again.
items.outcome: Enacted in 2002 after commercial terrorism coverage largely disappeared from the market post-9/11, TRIA has been renewed repeatedly on the same architecture: a $5 million per-event certification floor, a $200 million industry-aggregate trigger, an 80% federal cost-share above each insurer's deductible, and a $100 billion total program cap that has never been reached.
items.relevance: Two triggers, a per-event floor and an annual aggregate floor, keep a federal backstop out of routine losses and in reach of a real tail event.

items.name: CCRIF SPC parametric catastrophe pool
items.mechanism: Each member government pays CCRIF a premium for a policy that pays out automatically once an independent model of a specific earthquake's or storm's physical parameters, not surveyed damage, crosses a pre-agreed trigger; CCRIF can then verify the trigger and transfer funds within days instead of the months or years a loss-adjusted claim takes. Because the payout is fixed by the model and the trigger rather than actual losses, CCRIF never faces open-ended damage assessments, but a member can also be paid far less than its real loss if the model's parameters don't fully capture what happened on the ground.
items.outcome: CCRIF transferred Haiti's full US$7,753,579 payout within about a day of the January 12, 2010 earthquake, roughly 20 times the US$385,500 premium Haiti had paid, but that payout was a small fraction of total damage that was widely estimated in the billions of dollars, illustrating the basis-risk gap between a fast, formula-based parametric payout and a country's actual reconstruction need. Where it broke: The parametric trigger paid out exactly what the model said it should, fast, but the model's earthquake parameters did not scale with the true scope of Haiti's damage, so the country that most needed the money got a payout worth a small fraction of its loss even though the mechanism worked exactly as designed.
items.relevance: An index-triggered payout arrives in a day but only covers the loss the index tracks; test the index against real overruns before relying on it.

items.name: International Group of P&I Clubs pooling agreement
items.mechanism: A shipowner's own club pays the first US$10 million of a large claim alone; above that, the claim is shared across all 12 clubs through the pooling agreement up to US$100 million total, so no single club is wiped out by one member's catastrophic loss. Above the pool layer, Hydra (a Bermuda-domiciled captive reinsurer the Group itself owns, structured with a separate segregated cell for each club) retains a further slice before commercial market reinsurance takes the remaining tail, so the clubs mutually reinsure each other before ever paying a commercial reinsurer.
items.outcome: For the 2026/27 policy year, each club still retains the first US$10 million of a claim itself, the pool shares the US$10-100 million layer across all 12 clubs, and Hydra's own retained deductible in the layer above that was set at US$103.6 million, down from US$107.1 million the prior year as the clubs' claims experience improved.
items.relevance: Layer the pool: each member keeps the first slice, a shared layer with a hard ceiling pays the middle, and a jointly owned reinsurer and the market take the top.

items.name: UK Regulated Asset Base model (Sizewell C)
items.mechanism: Consumers pay a levy during construction (0.3p/kWh on UK bills as of Dec 2025), giving investors early revenue and a regulated, lower cost of capital in exchange for consumers absorbing bounded overrun risk.
items.outcome: Live on UK bills. The National Audit Office's modeling found that cutting the required investor return from 9% to 6% is worth as much as absorbing a 75–100% construction overrun; critics call the structure an open cheque book for developers.
items.early_vs_late: Risk shifts to all current ratepayers collectively and continuously; no order positions.
items.relevance: De-risking capital can be worth more than the overrun itself, which is why a credible insurance layer lowers LCOE even if it never pays out.

items.name: Vogtle 3 & 4 and the Westinghouse fixed-price collapse
items.mechanism: Westinghouse and CB&I held a fixed-price EPC to design and build both units, concentrating designer, constructor and project manager in one counterparty that absorbed all cost growth, until it filed for bankruptcy in March 2017 and the owners had to take over management themselves.
items.outcome: Final cost roughly $32–35B against an original ~$14B. Georgia regulators let Georgia Power recover $7.56B of its ~$10.2B share from ratepayers while shareholders absorbed ~$2.6B. Unit 4 still came in ~30% cheaper than Unit 3, the cleanest twin-unit learning datapoint on record.
items.early_vs_late: A fixed four-owner consortium from the start; the split that mattered was shareholder versus ratepayer.
items.relevance: Why the pool spreads overruns across bounded layers held by different parties: piling the whole tail onto one fixed-price counterparty bankrupts that counterparty and costs more anyway.

items.name: Coastal Virginia Offshore Wind tiered overrun schedule
items.mechanism: Virginia's SCC (Dec 2022) approved a sliding overrun split for Dominion's $9.8B project: customers pay 100% of the first band ($9.8–10.3B), the split is 50/50 to $11.3B, the company pays 100% to $13.7B, and anything beyond goes to a future proceeding.
items.outcome: In force; cited by EFI's cost-stabilization paper as the model for a formal tiered risk schedule.
items.early_vs_late: Tiered by overrun magnitude, never by commitment timing.
items.relevance: A regulator has already approved an answer to how the pool's bands should escalate: define severity bands and assign each an explicit split.

items.name: ARC Act (introduced 2026)
items.mechanism: The bipartisan Accelerating Reliable Capacity Act (Sens. Risch and Gallego, reintroduced Feb 2026) would authorize up to $3.6B to offset cost overruns across three or more next-generation reactor projects, up to $1.2B per qualifying project, repurposing existing appropriations.
items.outcome: Introduced; no floor vote as of this capture.
items.early_vs_late: The backstop engages only once three or more projects exist, so federal capital is gated on a real orderbook forming, though the bill does not split funds by order position.
items.relevance: Live legislative traction for the exact backstop layer the proposal cards describe, with shared overrun capital conditional on aggregation.

items.name: Marsh insurance placement for TerraPower Kemmerer
items.mechanism: Broker Marsh placed construction-phase insurance for TerraPower's Natrium build in Wyoming, layering US, London and Bermuda commercial insurers on top of the traditional nuclear mutual pools.
items.outcome: Reported March 2026 as the first time a next-generation US nuclear plant gained direct access to the commercial insurance marketplace; limits and premium undisclosed.
items.early_vs_late: Single-project placement.
items.relevance: Commercial reinsurance is already willing to price FOAK advanced-reactor construction risk. A microreactor pool could attract layered private capacity once early units de-risk the design, instead of leaning on government indefinitely.

items.name: Price-Anderson sub-100 MWe tier structure and retrospective pool exemption
items.mechanism: 10 CFR 140.12 sets required public liability financial protection for reactors above 10 MWt but below 100 MWe at $185 per thermal kilowatt times a population factor of 1.0 to 2.0, bounded by a $4.5M floor and a $74M ceiling. Specifically, the $158M per-reactor retrospective deferred premium pool under 10 CFR 140.11(a)(4) attaches only to reactors rated 100,000 electrical kilowatts or more.
items.outcome: A 20 MWt NRC-licensed reactor at population factor 1.0 binds at the $4.5M floor (or $7.4M at 2.0). For two or more reactors at one location, 10 CFR 140.12(c) sets the site total at the highest single-unit amount. The $158.026M retrospective assessment applies only to reactors rated 100 MWe or more; the Part 57 proposal says NRC could set a lower financial-protection amount on a technical finding.
items.early_vs_late: Set by regulatory formula based on thermal size and local population density; independent of order vintage.
items.relevance: For NRC licensees, the sub-100 MWe tier avoids each licensee's separate contingent assessment for accidents at other covered reactors. Army-regulated Janus prototypes and DOE-authorized pilot reactors sit outside this NRC tier and instead use their federal authorization and indemnification routes.

items.name: Technology performance and availability warranty insurance
items.mechanism: Specialized insurance underwriting backstops technology efficacy and availability guarantees (>90% capacity factor) for first-of-a-kind and early-commercial clean firm generation. The policy pays debt service if the asset fails to achieve stated output or heat rate due to design deficiencies or unforeseen outages.
items.outcome: Transfers technology risk off the reactor vendor and offtaker balance sheets onto investment-grade reinsurance capacity, enabling non-recourse project financing for unproven archetypes.
items.early_vs_late: Priced per deployment batch; early FOAK units pay higher risk-adjusted premiums until operating hours validate availability metrics.
items.relevance: Closes the bankability gap for private-wire PPAs: offtakers and commercial lenders require guaranteed capacity factors before committing long-term cash flows.

items.name: Fleet decommissioning surety trust pool
items.mechanism: Under 10 CFR 50.75(c)(1), a small PWR is penalized by the instruction to substitute P = 1200 MWt, forcing a 20 MWt unit to certify the same $85.56M (1986 dollars, ~$200M+ today) as a 1200 MWt plant. A fleet captive or mutual surety trust pools decommissioning liability across multiple modular units, replacing cash escrows with pooled surety bonds or letters of credit.
items.outcome: Proposed in NRC Part 57 (Docket NRC-2025-0379) to scale decommissioning obligations to actual plant inventory and radionuclide risk rather than a rigid 1200 MWt table floor.
items.early_vs_late: Pooled across operating units; contributions scale with operating life and unit count.
items.relevance: Removes an upfront capital roadblock where mandatory regulatory decommissioning funds for a single microreactor would otherwise approach the capital cost of the unit itself.
